notes: Slot 4 = Communist Party of Uzbekistan under Rashidov (First Secretary since 1959). Real institutions where they existed: Veli Kayum Khan's émigré committee (0), Writers' Union (1), women's councils (3), Komsomol (5), republican KGB (7), SADUM in Tashkent (10), Council of Ministers under Qurbonov (13), trade unions (18), Turkestan Military District (22, commander not named), Manghit dynasty (23). Slot 6 = Moscow-installed hardline centralists; slot 15 = cotton nomenklatura. MD UZB sprites all depict post-1991 parties, so all icons are null.

0.name: Milliy Turkiston Birlik Qo'mitasi
0.text:
The National Turkestan Unity Committee is the main political body of the Central Asian emigration in Western Europe, led by Veli Kayum Khan, the Tashkent-born nationalist who headed the wartime Turkestan National Committee in Berlin. From West Germany it publishes the journal ‘Milli Türkistan’ and keeps contact with émigré communities in Turkey, the Middle East and the United States.

Its programme is an independent, anti-communist Turkestan uniting Uzbeks, Kazakhs, Turkmens, Kyrgyz and Tajiks under a strong national government aligned with the West, the only power it believes can break the Soviet empire. Inside the republic it is known only through rumour, foreign radio and KGB warnings, but its émigré networks give it a voice abroad.

1.name: O'zbekiston Yozuvchilar Soyuzi
1.text:
The Writers' Union of Uzbekistan is the republic's official literary institution and one of the most prestigious in Central Asia. First Secretary Sharof Rashidov, himself a novelist, once chaired it, and its ranks include the poetess Zulfiya, the playwright Komil Yashin and a generation of younger poets who fill the journals and publishing houses of Tashkent.

Beneath the official optimism it nurtures a cultural conservatism: reverence for Alisher Navoi and the classical heritage, defence of the Uzbek language and a respectful image of family, mahalla and village. It accepts Soviet power and Moscow's leadership but quietly resists Russification. Its leverage is prestige and the patronage of Rashidov, who protects writers who serve the republic's image.

2.name: Yangi jadidlar
2.text:
The New Jadids are a loose circle of young Uzbek poets, historians and teachers in Tashkent and Samarkand who see themselves as heirs of the Jadid reformers of the early century, Behbudiy, Fitrat and Cho'lpon, whose works remain largely unpublished. The patriotic and searching verse of poets such as Erkin Vohidov and Abdulla Oripov gives the mood its voice.

They want liberal reform within the Soviet system: freer expression, an honest history of Turkestan, modern education, the rule of law and an end to the cotton monoculture's grip on people's lives. They admire Western learning but are no émigré agents. Their leverage is moral and cultural, felt in universities, editorial boards and the kitchens of the Tashkent intelligentsia.

3.name: O'zbekiston Xotin-Qizlar Kengashlari
3.text:
The Women's Councils of Uzbekistan are the network of party-sponsored women's committees attached to factories, kolkhozes and local soviets, heirs of the Hujum unveiling campaign launched in 1927. Their most prominent patron is Yodgor Nasriddinova, Chairwoman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet and the highest-ranking woman in Central Asian politics.

They push a social-democratic agenda inside the Soviet framework: schooling and careers for girls, creches and maternity care, the fight against child marriage, polygamy and bride-price, and relief for women worn down in the cotton fields. Loyal to Moscow, they put pressure on local patriarchs and mullahs. Their leverage lies in the regime's need to show the world an emancipated Soviet East.

4.name: O'zbekiston Kommunistik Partiyasi
4.text:
The Communist Party of Uzbekistan is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party in the Uzbek SSR. Since 1959 it has been led by First Secretary Sharof Rashidov, a writer from Jizzakh and candidate member of the Politburo, who has made himself the indispensable broker between Moscow and the most populous republic of Central Asia.

The party preaches loyalty to Brezhnev and the friendship of peoples, while Rashidov presents Tashkent as the Soviet showcase to Asia and Africa. Its overriding task is cotton, the ‘white gold’ delivered in ever larger plans, alongside the rebuilding of Tashkent after the 1966 earthquake. Its power is total, resting on every appointment and on Rashidov's network of loyal regional clans.

5.name: O'zbekiston Lenin Kommunistik Yoshlar Ittifoqi
5.english: Leninist Communist Youth Union of Uzbekistan
5.text:
The Leninist Communist Youth Union of Uzbekistan enrols students, young workers and kolkhoz youth across the republic. After the 1966 earthquake it hosted brigades from every corner of the Union to rebuild Tashkent, and it now sends volunteers to reclaim the Hungry Steppe and students to the cotton fields every autumn.

Beneath the ritual lives a radical streak of young believers who take the revolution at its word: they attack bribery, bride-price, ‘feudal survivals’ and the mullahs, and demand faster industrialisation and promotion on merit rather than kinship. It is wholeheartedly pro-Soviet. Its leverage is numbers and energy, and the fact that it trains the cadres who will run the republic tomorrow.

6.name: Moskva ko'zi
6.text:
Moscow's Eye is the centralist bloc of hardliners in Tashkent, gathered around the Russian second secretary of the Central Committee, Slavic department heads, senior prosecutors and veteran cadres trained under Stalin. Their task, as Moscow sees it, is to keep watch over Rashidov's apparatus, its cotton figures and its appointments.

They demand ideological discipline, Russian as the language of advancement, firm action against religious survivals and ‘local nationalism’, and an end to the patronage and padded reports they suspect behind the republic's successes. They look for protection to the conservative wing of the Central Committee in Moscow. Their leverage is the personnel file and a direct line to the Kremlin.

7.name: O'zbekiston SSR Davlat Xavfsizlik Qo'mitasi
7.english: Committee for State Security of the Uzbek SSR
7.text:
The Committee for State Security of the Uzbek SSR is the republican arm of the KGB, headquartered in Tashkent. It monitors the foreign delegations that pass through the Soviet showcase capital, watches unregistered mullahs, émigré contacts and listeners to foreign radio, and keeps a close eye on the deported Crimean Tatars campaigning in the republic for their return home.

Its doctrine is vigilance against pan-Turkism, pan-Islamism, bourgeois nationalism and foreign intelligence, and absolute loyalty to the Union. Answering to Moscow as much as to Rashidov, it can protect or destroy any career. Its leverage lies in surveillance, informers and the files it quietly gathers on the republic's elite, the cotton barons included.

8.name: Eroniylar jamoasi
8.text:
The Irani Community is the Persian-speaking Twelver Shia minority of Samarkand and Bukhara, descended from Persians of Merv and Khorasan brought to the emirate as captives and settlers. Many hold Soviet careers and Russianised surnames, yet they remain a distinct community with their own quarters, family networks and memory of Iranian origins.

Their politics are communal and moderate: they want the right to hold Muharram rites, keep their few surviving places of worship and stay in touch with relatives in Iran without suspicion. They accept the Soviet order and are often well integrated into it. Their leverage is cohesion, education and a strong presence in Samarkand's trade, crafts and professions.

9.name: Muharram azadorlari
9.text:
The Muharram Mourners are the clandestine devotional circles of the Shia of Samarkand and Bukhara, who keep the passion of Imam Husayn alive in private courtyards since public processions were banned. Their gatherings bring together elderly reciters and a younger generation who learn the laments and the rites by heart.

Theirs is a militant, uncompromising faith: the Soviet state is an oppressor, the mufti's Sunni board has no authority over them, and true guidance comes from the great clerics of Najaf and Mashhad. They seek no accommodation with atheism. Small and watched, their leverage is fervour, secrecy and the ability to fill a courtyard with mourners at a single word.

10.name: O'rta Osiyo va Qozog'iston Musulmonlari Diniy Boshqarmasi
10.english: Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan
10.native_full: O'rta Osiyo va Qozog'iston Musulmonlari Diniy Boshqarmasi
10.text:
The Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan is the state-recognised Muslim board, seated in Tashkent and led since 1957 by Mufti Ziyauddin Babakhanov. It administers the registered mosques of five republics and the Mir-i Arab madrasa in Bukhara, publishes the journal ‘Muslims of the Soviet East’ and receives foreign Muslim delegations.

Its line is loyal and scripturalist: Islam reconciled with Soviet power, support for Soviet policy in the Arab world, and fatwas against shrine pilgrimage, lavish feasts and other ‘innovations’. It serves Moscow's diplomacy while preserving a minimum of religious life. Its leverage lies in its monopoly on legal Islam and its value as the Soviet Union's Muslim face abroad.
10.wiki: Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan

11.name: Qo'rboshilar avlodi
11.text:
The Sons of the Kurbashis are the heirs of the Basmachi commanders who fought Soviet power in the Fergana Valley and eastern Bukhara into the 1930s. Their core lives among the Uzbek refugees of northern Afghanistan and the Turkestani émigrés of Saudi Arabia, while sympathisers inside the republic keep the legend of Ibrahim Bek alive.

They dream of a holy war that would drive out the Russians and restore a Muslim Turkestan under sharia and a single Islamic ruler. They reject the Soviet mufti and regard both atheist communism and Western secularism as enemies of the faith. Their leverage is the memory of armed resistance and cross-border ties that could matter if the southern frontier ever ignites.

12.name: Yashirin hujralar
12.text:
The Hidden Hujras are the unregistered study circles of the Fergana Valley, Tashkent and Bukhara, where teachers instruct pupils in Arabic, the Qur'an and Hanafi law in private houses. Many of their teachers studied with Muhammadjon Hindustoniy, the elderly scholar of Dushanbe whose clandestine lessons have trained a generation of unofficial mullahs.

They seek a moderate religious revival: more mosques, legal religious schooling, the right to fast, pray and celebrate openly, and a society shaped by Islamic morality rather than state atheism. They avoid politics and violence and distrust both the official mufti and the zealots. Their leverage lies in the trust of believing families and a growing number of devoted students.

13.name: O'zbekiston SSR Ministrlar Soveti
13.english: Council of Ministers of the Uzbek SSR
13.text:
The Council of Ministers of the Uzbek SSR is the republic's government, chaired by Rahmonqul Qurbonov and directing the ministries of agriculture, water management, construction and industry from Tashkent. Its planners administer the post-earthquake rebuilding of the capital, the reclamation of the Hungry Steppe and the vast irrigation schemes along the Amu Darya and Syr Darya.

Its outlook is technocratic: growth through irrigation, mechanisation and new industry such as the Navoi and Almalyk combines, managed by engineers rather than ideologues. It bargains with Moscow's Gosplan over every target and investment. Its leverage lies in administration, expertise and control of budgets and supplies, without which neither the party's plans nor the harvest can be delivered.

14.name: Mahalla oqsoqollari
14.text:
The Mahalla Elders are the white-bearded aksakals who preside over the neighbourhoods of Uzbek towns and the quarters of its villages. Officially their mahalla committees are a minor tier of local administration, but in practice they settle disputes, organise weddings, circumcisions and funerals, direct hashar communal labour and decide whose family is respectable.

They guard a non-ideological conservatism: respect for elders, family honour, modest dress, hospitality and quiet piety, accommodating Soviet power as long as it leaves the household alone. They care little for Washington or Moscow and a great deal for the street. Their leverage is social control: in the mahalla nobody marries, builds or prospers without their blessing.

15.name: Paxta beklari
15.text:
The Cotton Beks are the barons of the Uzbek cotton economy: chairmen of giant kolkhozes and state farms, district party secretaries and ministry officials whose fortunes rise and fall with the harvest. Decorated as Heroes of Socialist Labour, they rule their districts like private domains, bound to the regional networks of Samarkand, Fergana and Tashkent.

They want what keeps them powerful: higher plans that bring higher bonuses, more irrigated land, fewer inspectors and the freedom to dispense water, jobs and favours. Ideology hardly interests them, though they speak its language fluently. Their leverage lies in delivering cotton to the Union and in the gifts and loyalty that flow upward to Tashkent and beyond.

16.name: Chorsu savdogarlari
16.text:
The Chorsu Traders are the merchants, middlemen and speculators of Tashkent's ancient Chorsu bazaar and the kolkhoz markets of Samarkand, Bukhara and Andijan. They sell melons, dried fruit, silk and private-plot produce, and act as outlets for the underground workshops that turn state materials into goods the shops never have.

They want freedom to trade, larger private plots, fewer price controls and an end to campaigns against ‘speculation’. They have no ideology but the bargain and no interest in either bloc except as a source of scarce goods. Their leverage is that half the republic, officials included, depends on their stalls and discreet connections.

17.name: Orol posbonlari
17.text:
The Guardians of the Aral are hydrologists, biologists and fisheries experts of the Uzbek Academy of Sciences and its Karakalpak branch in Nukus, who watch with alarm as the Amu Darya and Syr Darya are drained for cotton. Since the early 1960s the Aral Sea has been shrinking, and the fishermen of Muynak already feel the change.

They argue for a balance between irrigation and nature: limits on water diversion, drainage to stop salinisation, protection of the tugai forests and reserves such as Chatkal, and caution with pesticides. They are no dissidents, but they challenge the cotton lobby's figures. Their leverage is scientific authority, which planners in Moscow may one day be forced to heed.

18.name: O'zbekiston Kasaba Soyuzlari Respublika Soveti
18.english: Uzbek Republican Council of Trade Unions
18.text:
The Uzbek Republican Council of Trade Unions unites the workers of Tashkent's aircraft and textile plants, the Chirchiq chemical works, the Almalyk mines and the state farms. Like every Soviet union body it is a transmission belt of the party, managing social insurance, sanatoria, housing and holiday vouchers rather than organising strikes.

Within those limits it voices a labour socialism of its own: better pay for cotton workers and pickers, safer working conditions, more housing and kindergartens, and a fairer share of the republic's wealth for ordinary families. It is loyal to Moscow but presses the interests of Uzbek workers. Its leverage lies in its vast membership and its control of welfare funds.

19.name: Xo'jayev yo'li
19.text:
Khodjayev's Path is the national-communist outlook of Uzbek party intellectuals and historians who honour Fayzulla Khodjayev and Akmal Ikramov, the founders of Soviet Uzbekistan, both shot in 1938 and rehabilitated after Stalin's death. Their legacy is discussed cautiously in the Institute of History, in the party schools and among older cadres.

They want an Uzbek road to socialism: broader republican autonomy, Uzbek cadres in leading posts, Uzbek as a language of administration and a truthful history of the Turkestan republic and the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic. Marxist yet national, they reject both Western capitalism and Russian tutelage. Their leverage lies in the native intelligentsia and in Rashidov's own quiet promotion of Uzbek cadres.

20.name: Temur avlodlari
20.text:
The Heirs of Timur are a nationalist mood among Uzbek students, teachers and craftsmen of Samarkand and Shahrisabz who revere Amir Timur, the conqueror and builder of Samarkand, whom Soviet historians condemn as a feudal tyrant. They gather around the Timurid monuments and retell stories of a glorious state whose armies reached from Delhi to Anatolia.

Their nationalism is populist and aggrieved: they condemn the privileges of Russian settlers, the drain of cotton wealth to Moscow and the contempt of Slavic officials, and want Uzbeks to be masters in their own land. They trust neither superpower. Their leverage is emotional, for a crowd at a football match or a funeral can turn into a protest.

21.name: Turkiston legionerlari
21.text:
The Turkestan Legionnaires are veterans of the Wehrmacht's Turkestan Legion, raised from Soviet prisoners of war in 1942, in which Uzbeks served in large numbers. Those who escaped repatriation live in West Germany, Turkey and the United States; those who returned served long camp sentences and now live quietly in Uzbek towns and villages, marked as traitors.

Their hard core still clings to the wartime dream of a Greater Turkestan built on Turkic blood and anti-Bolshevism, an authoritarian national state that would purge Russians and communists alike. They are few, watched by the KGB and despised by most Uzbeks who fought in the Red Army. Their leverage lies only in émigré networks and the propaganda value of their grievances.

22.name: Turkestanskiy voyennyy okrug
22.text:
The Turkestan Military District is the Soviet Army command for the southern flank of Central Asia, headquartered in Tashkent. Since the Sino-Soviet border clashes of 1969 a new Central Asian district has taken over the Chinese frontier, leaving Turkestan to guard Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and the borders with Afghanistan and Iran with its motor-rifle divisions and air bases.

Its officer corps, overwhelmingly Russian and Ukrainian, sees the region as a strategic bastion facing Iran, Afghanistan and the Middle East. Loyal to the Soviet state above any republic, it disdains clan politics and local nationalism. Its leverage is decisive in any emergency: it holds the guns, the airfields and the frontier.

23.name: Mang'itlar sulolasi
23.text:
The Manghit dynasty ruled the Emirate of Bukhara from the 18th century until 1920, when the Red Army stormed the city and the last emir, Said Alim Khan, fled to Afghanistan. He died in exile in Kabul in 1944, and his descendants are scattered across Afghanistan, Turkey and the West, keeping the memory of the court alive.

Their cause is the restoration of a Muslim monarchy in Bukhara, with the emir as guardian of the faith and the ulama as pillars of the state, the order the Bolsheviks destroyed. Inside the republic the emirate is officially remembered as feudal tyranny, yet old Bukharans still speak of it. Their leverage is legitimacy: they hold the last dynastic claim to Bukhara.
